e.etymology: A spelling of Lavinia from the American South, shaped by Lou. In Virgil's Aeneid, Lavinia is the princess Aeneas marries; the name's meaning is unknown.
A respelling of Kurt, the German short form of Konrad, from Germanic kuoni, 'bold', and rad, 'counsel'. The spelling also leans on Kirk.
An American name of the 1960s built on the sounds of Denise and Janine, with the -een ending of Maureen and Colleen.
A respelling of Dwayne or Duane, from the Irish surname O Dubhain, 'descendant of Dubhan', a name built on dubh, 'dark, black'.
A pet form of Earl, from the English title, Old English eorl, 'nobleman, warrior'. In the American South around 1900 it was given to both boys and girls.
e.note: Sounds exactly like the word early.

e.etymology: An American name of the 1960s that joins the La- prefix to Vonda, a variant of Wanda.
A respelling of Brittany, the English name of the region of northwest France settled by Britons in the 5th century. Brittany became a popular American girls' name in the 1980s.
From Latin candidus, 'white, bright', the name of several early saints. George Bernard Shaw used it for the heroine of his 1894 play Candida.

assoc.t: Candida, the yeast behind thrush and yeast infections

e.note: Candida is the medical name of the yeast that causes thrush and yeast infections.

e.etymology: A variant of Sandra, the short form of Alessandra and Alexandra, from Greek alexein, 'to defend', and aner, 'man'.
A respelling of Janine, the French pet form of Jeanne, the feminine of Jean (John). It goes back to Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
From the state, which Ponce de León named in 1513 for Pascua Florida, 'flowery Easter', the Spanish name of the Easter season. It was a girls' name in the US in the 1800s.
namesakes: Florida Evans (the mother on the sitcom Good Times)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jeannette, the French pet form of Jeanne, the feminine of Jean (John), from Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'.
An elaboration of Rose or Rosa, from Latin rosa, the flower. It was used in the American South in the early 1900s.
A spelling of Tanisha, an African American name that spread in the 1970s after actress Ta-Tanisha appeared on the TV series Room 222. It fits the Ta- and -isha patterns of that era.
A respelling of Kathleen, the English form of Irish Caitlín, which is the Irish form of Catherine. Catherine has long been tied to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
A pet name made by doubling the initial D, used for Deborah, Diane, Deirdre, Dorothy and other D names.
Spanish, from San Juan, 'Saint John', with the diminutive ending -ita. In Mexican American families, especially in Texas, it often honors the Virgin of San Juan de los Lagos.
A feminine spelling of Billie or Billy, the pet form of William, from Germanic wil, 'will', and helm, 'helmet, protection'. It was favored in Texas and the South in the 1920s and 30s.
A respelling of Carrie, the pet form of Caroline, a feminine form of Charles, from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
An elaboration of Ida with the -ell ending, close to Idella. Ida comes from the Germanic element id, 'work, labor'.
An African American name of the 1970s that joins the Sha- prefix to the -nita ending of Anita and Juanita.
An American name of the early 1900s built on Verda or Verdie with the -ell ending. It was given to both boys and girls, mostly in the South.
A respelling of Tracy, an English surname from Norman villages named Tracy, 'estate of Thracius'. As a girls' name it also served as a pet form of Theresa.
A feminine form of Roland, from Germanic hrod, 'fame', and land, 'land'. Roland was Charlemagne's knight in the medieval French epic The Song of Roland.
Probably a shortened form of Althea, from Greek Althaia, linked to althos, 'healing'.
A respelling of Megan, a Welsh pet form of Meg, short for Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. By coincidence magen is Hebrew for 'shield', as in Magen David, the Star of David.
A respelling of Phyllis, Greek for 'foliage'. In Greek myth Phyllis dies of love and becomes an almond tree.
A joining of Sue and Ellen. Suellen O'Hara is Scarlett's younger sister in Gone with the Wind, and the name peaked in the US just after the 1939 film.
A Roman family name of unknown meaning, borne by the emperor Otho, who ruled for three months in AD 69. In the Middle Ages Otho was also the Latin spelling of Otto, from Germanic aud, 'wealth'.
A phonetic spelling of Katherine as it was often said in the 19th-century US, in two syllables. Katherine comes from Greek Aikaterine and has long been tied to katharos, 'pure'.
An English surname with more than one source: a form of Noel, given to children born at Christmas, and a form of Neville, from a Norman place name meaning 'new town'.
